title: When Making Decisions, Acknowledge What You Don’t Know First
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that poor decisions usually trace to something the decision-maker did not know they needed to know. The post rejects two obvious fixes: waiting until every fact is in, which paralyzes, and collecting as much data as possible, which overwhelms. Its alternative is to use uncertainty as a tool by explicitly stating what you do not know before deciding. Brainstorming with colleagues about the gaps focuses information gathering on what matters. The author notes that this first step seems intuitive yet is routinely skipped.
points: Bad decisions most often reflect a missing piece of knowledge the leader did not realize was needed.
Waiting for complete information paralyzes, and gathering maximal data overwhelms the process.
Naming explicitly what you do not know focuses the search on the answers that matter most.
Brainstorming the gaps with colleagues streamlines information gathering and adds clarity.
Most decision-makers dive straight into their process and skip this simple, intuitive step.
quotes: Bad decisions are usually a reflection of something they didn’t know that they needed to know.

The solution is not to delay making a decision until all stones have been uncovered and every piece of information or data has been explored. Such an approach paralyzes decision-makers and prevents them from making decisions in a timely fashion.

Nor is the answer to the dilemma of not knowing to collect as much information as possible. Too much data can overwhelm the decision-making process and point decision-makers toward issues that are unimportant or tangential to the task at hand.
Clearly articulating what they need to know that they don’t know allows decision-makers to find the exact answers and information they need most.
Brainstorming with colleagues to identify what the decision-makers need to know and what they don’t is a critical first step.
Instead, they dive right into their process and fail to identify the knowledge they must have to make a great decision.
